papers.file: D:\Data\Harold\EvidenceBasedDB\Papers\An introduction to Unconventional Computing - QCi 202408 Medium.pdf
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc. educational blog lesson (Medium, Aug 26, 2024) that defines unconventional computing and motivates the company's EQC and reservoir hardware.

assertions.value: The authors define unconventional computing, for the purposes of the lesson, as any computing done in a way that is not the usual way, and keep the definition informal.
assertions.anchor: Computing in new and creative ways, p.2
quotes: Unconventional computing is any type of computing done in a way that is not the usual way.
it makes sense to keep the way unconventional is defined somewhat informal
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own working definition in the opening section.

assertions.value: The authors state that a computer with a few cooperating processors, or one that uses trinary variables in place of binary ones, is not very unconventional, because the basic concept stays the same; they are interested in significantly different computing, for example where no clear CPU processes the information.
assertions.anchor: Computing in new and creative ways, p.2
quotes: having a few processors that work together isn’t that unconventional
wouldn’t be very unconventional. The basic concept is the same, just a detail is different.
where there is no clear CPU processing the information
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of the term in the opening section.

assertions.value: The authors give systems designed to act directly as neural networks as an example of unconventional computing, with clear structure and logic that does not fit the conventional computing framework.
assertions.anchor: Computing in new and creative ways, p.2
quotes: Systems designed to act directly as neural networks are one example where there is clear structure and logic, but it doesn’t fit into the conventional framework for computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's illustrative example in an educational blog; no evidence is given.

assertions.value: The authors describe conventional computers as having a CPU that performs logical operations on information stored in memory, processing information centrally and sequentially by mathematical and logical rules, using electricity in semiconductor systems.
assertions.anchor: Computing in new and creative ways, p.1-2
quotes: performs logical operations on information stored in memory
information is processed centrally in a sequential way based on mathematical and logical rules
this is all done using electricity in semiconductor systems
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the baseline model they contrast against, in the opening section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the lesson does not cover the entire field of unconventional computing, and that it focuses on efforts relevant to the company's products and which may be practically useful; they note that many efforts in the field aim to push the boundaries of understanding of what a computer can be rather than to improve performance.
assertions.anchor: Computing in new and creative ways, p.2
quotes: this lesson will not cover the entire field of unconventional computing
many efforts where the goal is not so much to improve performance but to push the boundaries of our understanding of what a computer can be
We will rather focus on those which are relevant to our products, and which may be practically useful.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limits of the lesson's coverage.

assertions.value: The authors state that for most tasks conventional computers work just fine, and that the practical case for unconventional computing is limited to tasks where the conventional approach struggles.
quotes: for most tasks conventional computers work just fine
The practical case for unconventional computing is that there are some tasks where the conventional approach struggles
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim in an educational blog; no evidence is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors concede conventional computers suffice for most tasks, which limits the scope of any advantage claimed for QCi hardware.

assertions.value: The authors describe the graphics card as a historical example of an unconventional idea: a chip with many processors, each with a small amount of memory, calculates different parts of an image in parallel, because a single processor struggles to keep up; they state that modern computers still keep conventional CPUs for tasks not suited to massive parallel processing.
quotes: It is hard for a single processor to keep up with these, even if it is very fast.
calculate different parts of the image in parallel with a chip that has many processors, each with a small amount of memory
modern computers still have more conventional central processing units to perform all of the other tasks that are not well suited to massive parallel processing
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's illustrative historical account in an educational blog; no evidence is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that, given how widespread GPUs are, it is probably debatable whether GPU computing can still be considered unconventional, but that it was certainly an unconventional idea at one time.
quotes: it is probably debatable whether GPU computing can really still be considered “unconventional”
it was certainly an unconventional idea at one time
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's opinion in an educational blog.

assertions.value: The authors state that QCi's unconventional computers address tasks where conventional techniques struggle: hard optimization problems with the EQC (entropy quantum computing) paradigm, and machine learning with minimum training in the reservoir paradigm.
quotes: QCi’s unconventional computers address different tasks where the more conventional techniques struggle.
solving hard optimization problems, with the EQC (entropy quantum computing) paradigm
performing machine learning with minimum training in the reservoir paradigm
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing the intended use of its own products; no evidence is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson reports no benchmark, so the claim is of intended applicability only.

assertions.value: The authors present entropy quantum computing (EQC) as a form of unconventional computing, in the caption of a figure showing an example realization.
quotes: An example realization of entropy quantum computing, a form of unconventional computing
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's own classification of its product in a figure caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that defining a computer by a fixed list of conventional conditions does not work for unconventional computing, and that requiring a computer to be universal is too limiting, because a computer that is good at one particularly important problem could be useful without being universal.
quotes: This notion does not work in unconventional
Another option would be to require a computer to be universal, capable in principle of performing any computation given enough time.
an unconventional computer that is good at solving one particularly important problem could be useful without being universal
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's argument in an educational blog.
assertions.reader_inference: The page break splits the first quote's sentence; the quote is the part on the first page.

assertions.value: The authors cite analog tide predicting machines as a historical example of a computer that could perform only a very specific but highly important computation.
quotes: A historical example here is analog tide predicting machines, which only could perform a very specific but highly important computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's historical example, with no citation in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that, according to researchers on the topic, computation relies on an abstract model of what the system is doing, where information is programmed into the system and eventually read out, with the physical system acting as a stand-in for the model; so almost anything can be a computer if it is used as one, but just existing does not make a system a computer.
quotes: computation relies on having an abstract model of what the system is doing where information is programmed into the system and eventually read out
with the physical system acting as a stand-in for the model
almost anything can be a computer if it is used as one but just existing doesn’t make a system a computer
assertions.certainty_reason: A view attributed to unnamed researchers; no reference is given in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not carry the hyperlink, so the source of the researchers' answer cannot be read here.

assertions.value: The authors give a rock in the front yard as a reductio: without a limit on the definition, a rock could be called a computer that efficiently calculates the thermal equilibrium behavior of a rock but is not good at computing anything else.
quotes: otherwise we could say that a rock in the front yard is a type of computer that does a very efficient job of calculating the thermal equilibrium behavior of a rock
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's illustrative argument.

assertions.value: The authors state that some of the earliest ideas of reservoir computers treated the reservoir as a literal bucket of water, and that QCi's reservoir computer product uses a photonic system that is somewhat more complex than a bucket of water.
quotes: some of the earliest ideas of reservoir computers considered the reservoir to be a literal bucket of water
We offer a reservoir computer as one of our products, but it uses a photonic system that is somewhat more complex than a bucket of water.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product; the history of reservoir computing is stated without citation.

assertions.value: The authors define a probabilistic computer as one whose actions are well-defined but which has an element of randomness in how it behaves, in contrast to a deterministic computer, for which a given input gives a set series of events and any deviation is an error; they avoid the term non-deterministic because it has a particular meaning in complexity theory.
quotes: Conventional computers, like the one you are probably using to read this article, are deterministic.
any deviation from this behavior is an error
We will call this a probabilistic computer, while intentionally avoiding the term “non-deterministic”
since that has a particular meaning in complexity theory
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define their own term in the Probabilistic Computers section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the most conventional way to perform probabilistic computation is to use a deterministic computer with randomly generated numbers as inputs, that the Monte Carlo family of methods shows random choice is useful in conventional computing, and that one QCi product is a random number generator that does exactly this.
quotes: there are many cases even in conventional computing where making a random choice is useful
The most “conventional” way to perform probabilistic computation is to use a deterministic computer
One of our products is a device that does exactly this, a random number generator.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum mechanical processes are fundamentally probabilistic because of how quantum measurement works, and that their EQC paradigm is one example of fundamentally probabilistic computing.
quotes: Since quantum mechanical processes are fundamentally probabilistic (thanks to how quantum measurement works), our EQC paradigm is one example of fundamentally probabilistic computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor classifying its own paradigm; no evidence is given in the lesson.

assertions.value: The authors state that conventional computers are digital, with ones and zeros defined as voltages within certain ranges separated by a range of forbidden voltages, and that a classical computer whose allowed states are continuous would be an analog computer with values that change continuously over time.
quotes: Conventional computers are digital, meaning that the whole computational process can be described in terms of discrete 1 and 0 variables
ones and zeros as voltages being within certain ranges that are separated by a range of voltages that are considered “forbidden”
A classical computer where the allowed states are continuous would be an analog computer
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the digital and analog terms they use in the section.

assertions.value: The authors state that a digital computer switching must pass a voltage through the forbidden values, but that this happens quickly and in a way that does not interfere with other operations, so the model can be discrete and treat the change as instantaneous.
quotes: even a digital computer would have to have a voltage pass through the forbidden values
this happens quickly, in a way that does not interfere with other operations
this model can be discrete and treat the change as instantaneous
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's simplified explanation in an educational blog.

assertions.value: The authors state that the closest analogy to digital computing in a quantum setting is gate-model quantum computing, where discrete quantum operations (gates) are defined similarly to operations in conventional digital computers.
quotes: The closest analogy to digital computing in a quantum setting is gate-model quantum computing, where discrete quantum operations (gates) are defined similarly to the operations performed in conventional digital computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's characterization in an educational blog.

assertions.value: The authors state that their core technology could be used to build gate-model computers, but that there are also numerous more unconventional ways to use it; they state that more unconventional models can be less demanding in terms of noise levels and less demanding for the technology, so they are the company's current focus.
quotes: While our core technology could be used to build gate-model computers
there are also numerous more unconventional ways in which it can be used
More unconventional models can be less demanding in terms of noise levels and less demanding for the technology, so they are our current focus.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own technology and strategy; no evidence is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson states no demonstration of a gate-model machine on the core technology; 'could be used' is a capability claim only.

assertions.value: The authors state that computing on a discrete state space but continuously in time is a uniquely quantum proposition: classically a bit either flips or does not, and a state between 0 and 1 would make the computer analog, whereas quantum mechanically a superposition can be changed continuously over time.
quotes: Computing on a discrete state space, but in a way that is continuous in time is a uniquely quantum proposition.
Classically, if a bit is in the state 1, then it either flips to state 0 or it doesn’t
Quantum mechanically, however, it is possible to continuously change a superposition over time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's explanatory claim in an educational blog; no proof is given.

assertions.value: The authors give an example of a qubit state in which a and b change continuously, subject to normalization requiring the squared magnitudes to sum to one at all times, with a(0)=1 and b(0)=0 initially and b(1)=1 and a(1)=0 after some time, effectively flipping a bit over time; a measurement at any time finds outcome 0 with probability the squared magnitude of a(t) and outcome 1 with probability the squared magnitude of b(t), and no other outcome. The state definition itself did not render in the text layer.
quotes: a(0)=1 and b(0)=0 and after some time b(1)=1 and a(1)=0, effectively flipping a bit over time
I will always find a 0 outcome with probability ∣a(t)∣² and a 1 outcome with probability ∣b(t)∣² and there is no chance of any other outcome
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked illustration whose defining equation did not render in the text layer; no theorem is stated.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson itself says some math does not render on Medium; the full equations are on the QCi website.

assertions.value: The authors state that this continuous change differs fundamentally from a classical probability distribution that changes continuously overall while the underlying system undergoes discrete jumps, and that such hidden variable models are not possible in general for quantum systems.
quotes: This is fundamentally different from a classical probability distribution, which may change continuously overall.
such hidden variable models are not possible in general for quantum systems
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement without proof or citation in the lesson.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer joins two sentences across a line break; the quote is the part on one line.

assertions.value: The authors state that in a continuous-time quantum walk, Hamiltonian elements that flip bit values and terms that describe an optimization problem are active at the same time; it is digital in that there are two discrete outcomes and analog in that the operation is continuous and the state is well-defined at all points, so continuous-time quantum computing has properties of both, which would not be allowed in a non-quantum setting.
quotes: The simplest example is a continuoustime quantum walk, where Hamiltonian elements that flip bit values as well as terms that describe an optimization problem are active at the same time.
continuous-time quantum computing is somewhere between analog and digital, it has a combination of properties of both which would not be allowed in a non-quantum setting
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's characterization in an educational blog; no derivation is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints 'continuoustime' without its hyphen.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that conventional computers are very powerful but have limited capabilities on some tasks, such as optimization and machine learning, for which unconventional ways of thinking about computing are needed; they state that quantum systems provide new ways to compute based on the continuous nature of quantum superpositions, and that QCi's technology showcases some of these ways.
quotes: there are some tasks where computing capabilities are still limited
such as those in optimization and machine learning, unconventional ways of thinking about computing are needed
quantum systems provide new ways to compute, based on the continuous nature of quantum superpositions
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's conclusion about its own approach; the lesson reports no measured results.
assertions.reader_inference: The lesson contains no benchmark or experiment; its conclusions are conceptual and promotional.

assertions.value: The authors note that some of the math does not render correctly on Medium, and that the full editable equations are in the lesson on the company website.
quotes: Please note that some math doesn’t render correctly on Medium.
For the full editable equations, visit the lesson on our website here.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of this version of the lesson in its header note.
